newsitem.title: USA: Fed says giving weight to variety of price gauges.
newsitem.headline: Fed says giving weight to variety of price gauges.

text.p: The Federal Reserve will be paying attention to a number of gauges of inflation, given flaws in the Consumer Price Index, the central bank said Wednesday.

"In view of the remaining difficulties of accurately measuring price change in a highly complex and rapidly changing economy, alternative price indexes will continue to be given substantial weight, along with the CPI, in monitoring porgress toward the long-run goal of price stability," the Fed's Board of Governors said in their "Monetary Policy Report to Congress."
The report accompanies Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenpsan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

The Fed is expecting the CPI over the next year to come in slightly below the 3.2 percent rate recorded in 1996 on a fourth-quarter to fourth-quarter basis. It projects a rise in the index of 2.75 percent to 3.0 percent for 1997, which it said would be mainly due to a more favorable outlook for food and energy prices.
Still, the Fed saw "some risk" that the core CPI, which excludes food and energy, could edge higher in the coming year.

"The minimum wage will be moving up further in 1997, compounding whatever cost pressures might be in train as a result of labor market tightness," the Fed said, adding that it was uncertain how much of the increases in labor costs businesses would be able to absorb without raising prices.
The Fed pointed out that some broad measures of inflation derived from the gross domestic product accounts slowed in 1996.
However, it said it was concerned that even if the overall CPI decelerates this year, other price indices could suggest a pickup, reflecting pressures on productive resources.
